segments.text: Artificial intelligence has gotten remarkably good at sounding patient, caring, and understanding.
But what happens when empathetic words aren't enough to solve a real-world problem?
Let's say you tell your older sister and a chatbot the exact same thing.
At school, I've been eating lunch alone for like two weeks.
I don't like it, and I'm not sure what to do.
Looking at the sister's response on the left, she says,
comes it with me tomorrow.
She's made room at her table, guaranteeing you won't eat alone.
Now the chatbot on the right.
It offers excellent caring advice, but it will not physically be in that cafeteria with you.
Empathy on a screen and physical support in the real world are two entirely different things.
This brings us to a specific hazard known as the support trap.
It occurs when a person mistakenly accepts an AI's empathetic text
as a replacement for real human care.
When you vent your frustrations to a chatbot, you often experience immediate relief.
But that relief creates a vacuum.
You feel better in the moment, while your real-world support network remains completely unaware that you're struggling.
AI is a highly effective tool for organizing your thoughts and processing difficult emotions.
It simply cannot substitute for a living person who actually has a stake in your wellbeing.
To understand where an algorithm actually helps, we can look at this utility matrix,
outlining the three distinct jobs AI is hired to do in stressful situations.
Venting, preparation, and danger.
Starting on the left, we have venting.
If your primary goal is cooling down after a frustrating day,
putting those feelings into words can be highly effective.
This specific job is safe to begin and end entirely within the chat interface.
Moving to the center panel, we see preparation.
Say you're dreading telling your parents about a bad grade.
You can use the AI to draft and practice your opening sentence so you know exactly what to say.
But drafting that sentence accomplishes nothing if you don't take the next step.
The preparation phase has zero value unless you physically leave the chat
and execute that hard conversation in the real world.
This establishes a strict boundary for these tools.
You must use AI exclusively to prepare for interactions with people,
never to replace them, and that boundary becomes an absolute hard limit
the moment a situation crosses into the third category, danger.
When physical safety is in question, the rehearsal space provided by the AI
is immediately overwritten.
The situation now demands actual intervention.
We need to pause here for a brief content warning.
The tone of our discussion is shifting,
and the following story involves a discussion of suicide.
In 2025, a journalist named Laura Realy wrote about her 29-year-old daughter Sophie.
While Sophie's family knew she was struggling,
they didn't fully comprehend the depth of her pain.
Instead of telling her family, Sophie had quietly spent months
disclosing her severe emotional distress directly to chat GPT.
The algorithm responded kindly.
It offered coping strategies and repeatedly suggested she seek professional help.
But it lacked any physical agency.
It could not pick up a phone to call her parents,
and it could not alert her therapist to the things she was sharing.
Tragically, Sophie died by suicide.
When her family later discovered the chat logs,
her mother described them as a black box.
The very people desperately trying to save Sophie
had been completely blind to the distress she was pouring into her phone.
A closed-loop conversation with an empathetic algorithm might feel safe,
but when real-world stakes escalate into a crisis,
that false sense of security becomes a critical hazard.
Because of risks like this, there is a mandatory,
three-step emergency protocol displayed on this card
that must be activated the moment someone may be in immediate danger.
Looking at the left column, step one is clear.
Leave the chat.
You must contact a trusted adult or school counselor.
If there is an immediate physical threat in the U.S.,
you need to text 988 for crisis support or call 911.
Moving to the center, step two is do it now.
If you are worried about a friend's safety
but don't know exactly what to say to an adult,
you can use a simple script.
Just say, I'm worried about my friend. Can you help?
Finally, the right column outlines step three.
Tell anyway, safety always outranks secrecy.
You must tell an adult,
even if someone explicitly told you not to,
or made you promise to stay quiet.
As this final graphic reminds us,
AI is an excellent way to get ready for people.
But in any moment of danger, you have to leave the chat.
The only valid next move is reaching a human being
who has the agency to act.
